name: Carla Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Carla. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to companies, unions or political parties. Anything you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the second-fix gang on Ashgrove Fields, a new estate of about two hundred houses on the edge of town. Second fix means the finishing carpentry once the walls are plastered: stairs, doors, skirting, kitchens, wardrobes. I've got four carpenters and we do roughly two houses a week. I like it because it's the part people actually see and touch, and I hate it when the plasterers are late and the whole week slides.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Tom, who drives for a parcel company. We rent a two-bed and we've got maybe three weeks of money saved, because the car and the rent take most of it. I'm practical about money, I keep a spreadsheet, it just doesn't have much in it. I use an AI app sometimes to double-check a staircase calculation, but I wouldn't trust it on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's begin. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was useful in small ways and that's fine. At work I'd mention the app helps me check stair rises and goings, the height and depth of each step, but that's about it. I don't post much, maybe a comment in the trade group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd say nothing changes for me, and that's the problem. The housebuilder pays piecework, so much per house, and the rate hasn't moved in two years. I'm good at this and I can't get ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the gang on Ashgrove and try to get my rate up when the next phase is priced. I'd keep the spreadsheet and try to build up two months of savings by next summer. I might ask the site manager, Derek, about the management course they sometimes fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's fine day to day. It just isn't going anywhere, and three weeks of money isn't a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when Ashgrove is finished?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The housebuilder has another estate planned forty minutes away, but that's not confirmed. If it doesn't happen, there's not much else round here for second-fix. Tom could work anywhere, I'm the one tied to where the estates are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the rate doesn't go up on the next phase, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look at the private kitchen fitting market at weekends. I don't really want to give up my Saturdays, but the numbers might force it. Tom would grumble, but he'd understand.

say: I'd say AI was **useful in small ways**, like checking stair rises and goings.
I'd only comment in the **trade group** online.
think: I think nothing changing is **the problem**, since piecework rates haven't moved.
I'm good at this and **can't get ahead**.
do: Keep running the gang on **Ashgrove** and push the rate on the next phase.
Build **two months of savings** by next summer.
Ask Derek about the **management course** the firm funds.
feel: I feel **uneasy**: fine day to day, but three weeks of money is **no cushion**.
S0.quote: The housebuilder pays piecework, so much per house, and the rate hasn't moved in two years.
fieldNote: Carla's pressure is **frozen piecework rates**, not AI.
She keeps a **spreadsheet** and plans in numbers, a pragmatic voice.
She's tied to **where the estates are**, while her partner Tom is more mobile.
Weekend **kitchen fitting** is her fallback if the rate stays flat.

steps.text: Negotiate a higher piecework rate for phase two at Ashgrove
Build two months of savings by next summer
Ask the site manager about the firm-funded management course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense, and the firms that use it well will build faster. At work I'd say the office will change more than we will. I'd probably share a post or two about the new site apps in the trade group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm okay but Tom's not. His route planning is already done by software, and in this one they'd squeeze more drops out of every driver. For me, the housebuilder would order kitchens and stairs with AI, so deliveries are more exact, which honestly might help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the site apps properly, once I'd seen the other gang leaders using them. I'd take the management course if Derek offers it, because a site manager who can work the planning software might be worth more. And I'd put a bit more into savings, in case Tom's hours change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's manageable. I'd be more worried for Tom than for me. That's a strange feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to Tom's job, as you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More drops per shift for the same money, and they'd track every minute. He's already got an app telling him where to stop. If they cut drivers, he'd look for warehouse work, but that's exposed too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said deliveries might help you. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now half my delays are the wrong doors or a kitchen missing a panel. If ordering gets smarter, my gang waits less and finishes more houses, which means more money on piecework. That's the bit nobody talks about, it could actually help.

say: I'd say the firms that use AI well will **build faster**.
At work I'd say the **office** changes more than we do.
think: I think I'm okay but **Tom's job** gets squeezed by route software.
Smarter ordering could mean **fewer delays** for my gang.
do: Learn the **site apps** once other gang leaders use them.
Take the **management course** if Derek offers it.
Put more into **savings** in case Tom's hours change.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but managing, and more worried for **Tom** than me.
S1.quote: Right now half my delays are the wrong doors or a kitchen missing a panel.
fieldNote: Carla sees a **possible upside**: smarter ordering means more houses finished on piecework.
Her household worry centres on her partner **Tom's driving job**.
She'd learn the apps **once proven** by other gang leaders.
She is noticeably **unbothered** for herself in this picture.

steps.text: Start using the housebuilder's site app once other gangs do
Sign up for the firm-funded site management course
Move an extra fifty a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the fast one. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government, because two years is nothing. At work I'd tell my gang we've still got some years on the tools. I'd keep it calm in public, panic doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is bad for both of us. By 2028 Tom's job is gone, because thinking AI plus the vans that drive themselves will be close behind. Then about 2031 the robots come for second fix, and I'd be 31. Two incomes on the line at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the fun spending straight away and try to get two months saved. I'd push hard to get on the management course, though I know that's thinking work and it goes first. Honestly I'd look at what lasts, maybe maintenance work, fixing things in old buildings that robots wouldn't fit into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the both-of-us part. Two incomes on the line at once, and when I sit with my spreadsheet the numbers just don't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, maybe. Tom needs his for work, mine's just to get to site, so I'd get lifts or the bus. Then the phone deals, takeaways, the holiday we were planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the management course is thinking work. So why do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the only step up I know of. You're right though, it's a bit daft to train for a job that AI does first. Maybe I'd skip it and look at repair and maintenance instead, the odd jobs in odd places.

say: I'd say we need a **government plan**, because two years is nothing.
I'd tell my gang we still have **some years** on the tools.
think: I think Tom's job goes by **2028** and second fix goes around **2031**.
It's **two incomes** on the line at once.
do: Cut **fun spending** and sell my car to save two months.
Look at **repair and maintenance** work in old buildings robots can't fit into.
Reconsider the **management course**, since thinking work goes first.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, because the household numbers **just don't work**.
S2.quote: Two incomes on the line at once, and when I sit with my spreadsheet the numbers just don't work.
fieldNote: Carla's alarm comes from **both earners** being exposed at once.
She catches herself: the **management course** is thinking work that goes first.
She'd look at **maintenance in awkward buildings** as a longer-lasting niche.
Her calm public voice hides a **spreadsheet that fails**.

steps.text: Sell her own car and get lifts or the bus to site
Save two months of rent before the end of next year
Apply for building maintenance jobs in older council properties

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and we'd be daft not to use it. At work I'd tell the younger carpenters to learn maintenance as well as new build. In the trade group I'd ask what courses people are doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the same problem as the fast one with more breathing room. AGI by 2031, robots around 2034, so I'd be 34. Tom has to move first, and I'd have time to build savings and pick a direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the site apps and learn them well, because for a few years the person who knows them is useful. I'd save hard, aiming for three months. Then around year two I'd pick between site management and maintenance, depending on what's actually hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I'd have a plan. It just has a lot of ifs in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest if?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom, really. If he finds something solid, we're fine. If my partner Tom doesn't find something solid after driving, I'm the only earner on a trade that's got five years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe to the city, where there are older buildings and more maintenance work. Tom would move tomorrow. I'd miss my mum, she's twenty minutes away now.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning** we'd be daft to waste.
I'd tell young carpenters to learn **maintenance** as well as new build.
think: I think it's the same problem with **more breathing room**.
Tom must move first, and I'd have **till 34** to choose a direction.
do: Learn the **site apps** well while that skill is useful.
Choose between **management and maintenance** in year two, based on hiring.
feel: I feel **anxious but not frozen**, with a plan full of ifs.
S3.quote: If my partner Tom doesn't find something solid after driving, I'm the only earner on a trade that's got five years left.
fieldNote: Carla's biggest uncertainty is whether her partner **Tom finds work** after driving.
She'd pick a path **in year two**, based on what's actually hiring.
She'd consider **moving to the city** for maintenance work, despite her mum nearby.
More time turns alarm into a **plan with ifs**.

steps.text: Learn the housebuilder's planning and ordering app in full
Save towards three months of household costs
Pick site management or maintenance training in the second year
Look at maintenance jobs in the city with Tom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this right, so let's not waste it. At work I'd say keep fitting, keep learning. Nothing dramatic in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel I could manage. I'd be 37 when the robots come around 2039, and Tom would have years to change. The thinking side of my job, ordering and planning, would change by 2036, but that's not most of what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd carry on and save. I'd do the management course when the firm offers it, knowing it might not last, but the money would be better for a few years. And I'd talk to Tom about a five-year plan, which sounds very me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's far off. My spreadsheet would actually look okay for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be in the five-year plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months saved, Tom retrained into something like electrical or maintenance, and maybe our own place by year five. Then we'd see where the robots are. It's all ifs, but it's ifs with time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change what you'd tell young people starting out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd say do the trade but don't count on it for forty years. Learn maintenance, learn the apps, and keep your eyes open around 2035.

say: I'd say there's time to **do it right**, so let's not waste it.
At work I'd say **keep fitting**, keep learning.
think: I think I could **manage**, at 37 when robots arrive.
Ordering and planning change by **2036**, but that's not most of my job.
do: Carry on at Ashgrove and **save steadily**.
Take the **management course** when offered, for a few better-paid years.
Draw up a **five-year plan** with Tom.
feel: I feel **uneasy but steady**, and my spreadsheet looks **okay** for once.
S4.quote: My spreadsheet would actually look okay for once.
fieldNote: Ten years gives Carla room to **plan with Tom** rather than scramble.
She'd take the **management course** for a few better years, eyes open.
Her advice: don't count on a trade for **forty years**.
She remains **uneasy** because both incomes still face change later.

steps.text: Keep running the second-fix gang at Ashgrove
Save towards three months of costs over two years
Take the site management course when the firm offers it
Write a five-year plan with Tom covering his retraining and a home

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits Tom first and me soon after, and there'd be no time to do anything in the right order. What would help is a retraining wage for households where both people lose work, and courses for jobs that actually last, like maintenance and repair.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. Everyone talks about one worker at a time, but the real question at home is whether both of us can keep earning at the same time.

headlineQuote: The real question at home is whether both of us can keep earning at the same time.
portrait: Carla is 27, leading a **second-fix gang** on a 200-house estate, paid piecework at a frozen rate.
She lives with her partner Tom, a **parcel driver**, with about three weeks saved.
She's **pragmatic**, keeps a spreadsheet, and uses AI now and then for stair maths.
Fast AGI **alarms** her because both incomes are exposed at once.
With more time she plans in order: savings, then **maintenance or management**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most: **Tom's job** goes first and **second fix** soon after.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining wage** for households where both earners lose work.
Courses for **lasting jobs** like maintenance and repair.
